name: Nora Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run sixty suckler cows, that means cows that raise their own calves, on about a hundred and ten hectares, and I make hay for the horse people round here. Winter days are feeding: I'm out at seven with the old tractor and a round bale on the spike, then mucking out the calf pens, then checking water. In the afternoon I do the herd book, by hand, in a green ledger my uncle started in 1988.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Frank left me the farm when he died two years ago. Before that I was a practice manager at a dental surgery for eighteen years, running rotas and chasing unpaid bills. Everyone expected me to sell, and I nearly did, but I walked the fields one evening and couldn't do it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still learning. I lost a calf in February because I didn't spot that the cow was in trouble soon enough, and I think about that more than I'd like. My neighbour Bill has been farming fifty years and he's patient with me, mostly, and my husband Pete fixes anything electrical, which on this farm is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, let the office people have their toy. It doesn't feed cows. I'd probably not say anything at all, actually, I don't do social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means nothing for me. I don't use AI, I don't trust it, and I don't need it to tell me a cow is lame. Frank ran this place with a ledger and a phone on the wall, and I'm doing all right with the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'd do anyway. Get the hay shed roof fixed before spring, which is about six thousand, and buy a better bull at the March sale. Keep the books in the ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like reading about a new phone I'm not going to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the dental practice we had a new booking system that was meant to be clever, and it double-booked a root canal with a child's check-up for a month. I spent weeks apologising to people in the waiting room. Since then I like things I can see working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your money situation, how does it sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable, I'll say that. Frank left the land with no debt, and we've got about a year of savings, plus Pete's wages. The mortgage is on our old house, which we let out now, so the rent covers it.

S0.say: I'd say fine, let the office people have their toy, because it doesn't feed cows. Honestly I'd probably say nothing, since I'm not on social media.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me, because I don't use AI and don't trust it. My uncle ran this place with a ledger and a phone on the wall, and I'm managing the same way.
S0.do: Fixes the hay shed roof before spring for about six thousand and buys a better bull at the March sale. Keeps the herd records in her uncle's handwritten ledger.
S0.feel: Calm, like reading about a new phone she isn't going to buy.
S0.quote: I don't need it to tell me a cow is lame.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is matter-of-fact and slightly impatient with the whole subject. Her distrust of AI comes from one specific bad experience with a booking system, which she still remembers in detail. Debt-free land and rental income make her secure, and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds about right, things never go as fast as the headlines say. A bit of help here and there and most people keep their jobs. I'd say that at the cattle mart and nobody would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the fewer beginners bit stings, because I'm a beginner at forty-three. Bill won't be around forever, and who teaches the next me? The young vet at our practice is the last trainee they took on, and she's brilliant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep going with Bill on Tuesday mornings, ask more questions, and maybe pay for a calving course at the agricultural college in February. I'm not going near any AI programs, slow or fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small worry for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the calf you lost.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was a big bull calf, coming backwards, and I waited too long because I thought I'd give her time. Bill would have had his arm in there an hour earlier. I sat in the pen afterwards and cried, and then I went in and wrote it in the ledger, because that's what Frank would have done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of this change what you tell Sophie and Ben about jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sophie's fifteen and wants to be a vet, so I'd tell her to keep at it, they still need hands on the animal. Ben's eleven and wants to drive tractors, which is fine by me. I wouldn't change anything I tell them for this picture.

S1.say: I'd say it sounds about right, because things never go as fast as the headlines say. A bit of help here and there and most people keep their jobs.
S1.think: Privately the fewer beginners part stings, because I'm a beginner at forty-three. My neighbour Bill won't be around forever, and I wonder who teaches the next person like me.
S1.do: Keeps learning from Bill on Tuesday mornings and pays for a calving course at the agricultural college in February. Stays away from AI programs entirely.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small worry for young people starting out.
S1.quote: I sat in the pen afterwards and cried, and then I went in and wrote it in the ledger, because that's what Frank would have done.
S1.fieldNote: The story of the lost calf came out with real feeling and shows how heavy her learning curve is. Her answer to change is a person, Bill, and a course, never a tool. She is level-headed about the scenario and saves her worry for the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides are shouting and neither has a plan. Some help for people who lose jobs, sure, but not a whole new system overnight. I'd keep my head down and get on with the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my old job at the dental practice would be gone. The rotas, the bills, the reminders, all of that is exactly what this card describes. My friend Janet still does it, and she's got a sick husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Janet, first thing, and tell her to start looking now, not when the letter comes. On the farm, nothing changes, though I'd hold off on the new bull if beef prices wobbled. I'd let the house rent keep covering the mortgage and leave the savings alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Sorry for Janet, glad I got out, and a bit cross that I'm glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think people would buy less beef if office workers were losing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the better cuts, yes. Steak is the first thing to go when money's tight, mince keeps selling. My calves go to a finisher who sells to butchers, so I'd feel it a year later in the price he offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the bull. That's a few thousand. How do you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Bill and look at what the finisher paid last autumn. If it's down more than ten percent, I'd use the old bull another year. He's slow but he's still doing his job, a bit like me.

S2.say: I'd say both sides are shouting and neither has a plan. I'd support some help for people who lose jobs, but not a whole new system overnight.
S2.think: Privately I think my old job at the dental practice would be gone, since rotas and bills are exactly this kind of work. My friend Janet still does it, and she has a sick husband.
S2.do: Rings her friend Janet straight away to urge her to start job hunting early. Keeps the old bull another year if the finisher's price falls more than ten percent, and leaves the savings alone.
S2.feel: Uneasy: sorry for Janet, glad she left, and cross with herself for being glad.
S2.quote: He's slow but he's still doing his job, a bit like me.
S2.fieldNote: Her centre politics come through as tiredness with both sides rather than any strong view. The concern for Janet is specific and practical. She thinks about prices in terms of the finisher's offer a year later, which shows she's learning the business quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to calm down and find a middle way. Tax the companies that make a fortune, a bit, and help the people who lose out, a bit, without wrecking the economy. That's what I'd say, and both sides would hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the house price part interests me. Our old house that we rent out would be worth more, and the land too. But if lots of professional people lose their jobs, who's going to keep horses and buy my hay? Half my hay customers are solicitors and accountants with ponies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Pete we sit tight. I wouldn't sell the house even if the price is silly, because the rent is safer than a lump of money in a crisis. I'd ring my hay customers in spring and offer a small discount for paying up front, to lock in the orders. And I'd grow a bit less hay and keep more grass for the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The money side looks fine, it's the not knowing that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hay customer do you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, who has three ponies for her daughters and pays me in cash every October with a box of biscuits. She's a lawyer in town. If her job goes, the ponies go, and that's three hundred bales I need to find a home for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. If it could find you new hay buyers, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd put a card in the feed shop window and ask at the riding school, same as Frank did. If that doesn't work, I'll feed the hay to my own cows.

S3.say: I'd say people need to calm down and find a middle way: tax the companies a bit and help the people who lose out a bit. Both sides would hate that, but I'd still say it.
S3.think: Honestly the rising value of our rented-out house and the land interests me. But half my hay customers are solicitors and accountants with ponies, and I wonder who'll buy hay if they lose their jobs.
S3.do: Keeps the rented house rather than selling into a boom and offers hay customers a small discount for paying up front in spring. Grows a little less hay and keeps more grass for the cattle.
S3.feel: Uneasy, not about the money but about not knowing.
S3.quote: If her job goes, the ponies go, and that's three hundred bales I need to find a home for.
S3.fieldNote: Nora is the rare farmer whose customers are exactly the professionals this card hits, through hay for their horses. She refuses AI even when it could help, preferring the feed shop window. Her politics are firmly in the middle and she seems proud of annoying both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot calve a heifer at two in the morning in the mud. People said milking robots would empty the countryside, and the dairy down the road still has three workers. Don't panic, is what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more worried than I'd let on. If the big beef feedlots, the huge yards where cattle are fattened, go fully robotic, they'll sell cheaper than me and I'm finished as a business. I'm slow at this already, and I'd be competing with something that's never slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy a robot, I know that much. I'd talk to Bill and the finisher about selling direct, maybe boxes of beef to local families, so I'm not just competing on price. And I'd ask Pete, since he's an electrician, whether he'd ever want to work on these machines, because that might be the job that lasts in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the beef price fell hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new tractor we've been saving for, about forty thousand, goes off the table. Then I'd sell ten of the older cows and run a smaller herd. I'd keep the hay going, because horses don't care about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'don't panic' in public but you're cutting the herd in private. Which one is true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I don't want the people at the mart frightened, half of them are seventy. But at home with my ledger I'd be doing the sums, quietly.

S4.say: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot calve a heifer at two in the morning in the mud. I'd tell people not to panic, because milking robots never emptied the dairy down the road.
S4.think: Privately I'm more worried than I'd let on, because robotic feedlots could undercut my beef. I'm slow at this already, and I'd be competing with something that's never slow.
S4.do: Rules out buying any robot and explores selling beef boxes direct to local families. Drops the forty-thousand tractor plan, sells ten older cows if prices fall, and asks her electrician husband about working on the new machines.
S4.feel: Anxious, though she insists she's stubborn rather than foolish.
S4.quote: I'll believe it when I see a robot calve a heifer at two in the morning in the mud.
S4.fieldNote: The gap between her public calm and her private sums is widest here, and she explained it as protecting older farmers at the mart. She still refuses the technology outright. The idea that her husband's electrical skills might be the household's lasting job was her own, and it surprised her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because that's the one where my beef is up against a factory. What would help is a simple label that says who raised the animal and where, so people can choose a farm with a person on it. And keeping the rules simple, because I spend enough evenings on paperwork.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the cows knowing my voice, honestly. Frank used to say they come to the gate for the bucket, not for you, but I think he was wrong.

headlineQuote: Frank used to say they come to the gate for the bucket, not for you, but I think he was wrong.
portrait: Nora Baker was a dental practice manager for eighteen years until her uncle left her his beef and hay farm, which she now runs with a handwritten ledger and a lot of help from her neighbour Bill. She is brisk, sceptical of hype and of both political sides, and has never used AI after a bad experience with a booking system. The office scenarios make her worry for an old colleague and for her hay customers, many of whom are professionals with ponies. In the robot picture she stays calm in public but privately fears robotic feedlots undercutting her, and plans to sell beef direct rather than buy a machine.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because her beef would be competing on price against robot-run feedlots.
whatWouldHelp: A simple label showing who raised the animal and where, so shoppers can choose farms with people on them, and simple rules that don't add paperwork.
